items.prompt: What is the main purpose of rejecting infeasible brute force before implementation?

options.text: Avoid spending implementation effort on a growth class that cannot satisfy the stated constraints.
Prove brute force is always conceptually wrong.
Choose shorter variable names.
Replace all reasoning with low-level optimization.

feedback.reason: Constraint analysis should eliminate impossible strategy classes early.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Derive the candidate's dominant work and storage, substitute the maximum input and output requirements, and compare those totals with explicit budgets. If the gap spans orders of magnitude, coding or micro-optimizing that strategy cannot close it; implementation effort should move to a structurally better class.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Reject a strategy from a concrete upper-bound calculation or an unavoidable resource limit. Do not confuse an expensive-but-required output enumeration with avoidable brute force.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.brute_force_never: Brute force can be appropriate for small inputs or required enumeration.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.names: Identifier length changes neither the candidate count nor the number of operations performed for each candidate.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.micro_optimize: Constant-factor tuning cannot repair an orders-of-magnitude growth mismatch.

items.prompt: Is an O(2^n) subset search automatically unacceptable?

options.text: No. It can be appropriate for small n or when all subsets must be output.
Yes. Exponential algorithms are never usable.
No. It is always acceptable.
It is acceptable only on sorted input.

feedback.reason: Feasibility depends on concrete n, per-state work, and whether enumeration is mandated.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

The state count is 2^n, but feasibility is a numerical question. At n = 20 it is about one million states before per-state work, while at n = 60 it exceeds 10^18. If every subset must be returned, Ω(2^n) enumeration is also imposed by the output contract.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Reject a strategy from a concrete upper-bound calculation or an unavoidable resource limit. Do not confuse an expensive-but-required output enumeration with avoidable brute force.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_bad: For n around 20, the state count can be manageable.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_good: Exponential growth makes the same method infeasible once n or per-state work crosses the available budget.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_sorted: Sorting can affect processing order but does not change that an n-element set has 2^n subsets.

items.prompt: For n = 100,000, why should an O(n²) pair check usually be rejected under ordinary contest-scale budgets?

options.text: It implies about 10 billion pair operations before overhead.
Because any nested loop is forbidden.
Because pairs cannot be represented.
Because both loops use the name n.

feedback.reason: Substituting the maximum constraint exposes a cost far above common abstract budgets.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Checking every ordered pair performs about n² = 10^10 comparisons; checking only unordered pairs still performs n(n−1)/2 ≈ 5×10^9. Both exceed an abstract 10^8-operation budget by large factors before comparison overhead, so the rejection follows from the count rather than nested syntax.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Reject a strategy from a concrete upper-bound calculation or an unavoidable resource limit. Do not confuse an expensive-but-required output enumeration with avoidable brute force.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.nested_syntax: Nested control flow can still have O(n) aggregate movement; only the derived pair count proves this candidate quadratic.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.pairs_output: Pairs are representable, but billions of examined pairs exceed the ordinary budget unless materializing them is required.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.variable_n: Using the same identifier in both bounds does not matter; the two independent ranges and maximum n determine the product.

constraints: Use the dominant count n² and ignore constant factors.

items.prompt: Why is enumerating all n! permutations usually rejected much earlier than enumerating all 2^n subsets?

options.text: Factorial growth overtakes exponential 2^n rapidly.
Permutation count is actually linear.
2^n is always larger than n!.
Permutations require sorting first.

feedback.reason: Factorial branching multiplies by a decreasing sequence n·(n-1)·...·1.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

A subset makes two include/exclude choices per element, giving 2^n states. A permutation has n choices for the first position, n−1 for the second, and so on, giving n!. The ratio n!/2^n eventually grows without bound, so factorial enumeration crosses practical budgets at much smaller n.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Reject a strategy from a concrete upper-bound calculation or an unavoidable resource limit. Do not confuse an expensive-but-required output enumeration with avoidable brute force.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.permutations_linear: Choosing a distinct element for every position produces n·(n−1)·…·1 = n! orderings, not n.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.subsets_more: For sufficiently large n, n! is much larger.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_required: The factorial count comes from arranging all elements; a preliminary sort neither creates nor removes those arrangements.

items.prompt: A branch-and-bound algorithm has a heuristic prune but no proof that it removes branches in the worst case. What worst-case class should still be considered?

options.text: The full brute-force search-tree class.
O(1) because pruning exists.
O(n) because each branch is visited once.
No worst-case analysis is possible.

feedback.reason: A heuristic can improve typical behavior without changing the formal worst case.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Worst case ranges over every valid input. If no invariant guarantees a prune, construct an input on which the heuristic rejects no branch; the algorithm then explores the original full tree. Observed average pruning may still matter operationally but cannot replace that worst-case upper bound.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Reject a strategy from a concrete upper-bound calculation or an unavoidable resource limit. Do not confuse an expensive-but-required output enumeration with avoidable brute force.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant: An input that defeats the heuristic can force exploration beyond one state, so pruning's existence does not imply O(1).
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.linear: Visiting each branch once is linear in the number of branches, but that branch count itself may be exponential in n.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.average_only: The unpruned tree gives a valid upper bound.

items.prompt: A task asks to list all n! permutations. Should O(n!) enumeration be rejected solely because it is factorial?

options.text: No. The output contract itself requires n! results, so factorial output work is unavoidable.
Yes. The requested output should be ignored.
A constant-time algorithm can return all results symbolically under the same materialized-output contract.
The best possible time is always O(n²).

feedback.reason: Avoidable brute force must be separated from mandatory enumeration.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Materializing every permutation requires writing n! result records and, if each record contains n elements, Θ(n·n!) output volume. No algorithm can satisfy that contract in sub-output time. Review should therefore minimize delay and overhead per result rather than reject the unavoidable enumeration class.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Reject a strategy from a concrete upper-bound calculation or an unavoidable resource limit. Do not confuse an expensive-but-required output enumeration with avoidable brute force.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_always: An algorithm cannot return all permutations without producing them.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant_possible: A symbolic descriptor would change the output contract; materialization must write every requested permutation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_n2: For growing n, n! requested results already exceed any universal O(n²) time bound.

items.prompt: An O(n³) algorithm is proposed for n = 400 under an abstract 100,000,000-operation budget. What first-pass conclusion follows?

options.text: 400³ = 64 million, so it is provisionally plausible before constants and memory review.
Reject every cubic algorithm regardless of n.
The count is about 64 quadrillion.
The count is constant because 400 is fixed in the statement.

feedback.reason: A higher-order polynomial can be feasible at a small enough maximum n.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Substitution gives 400³ = 64,000,000 abstract inner operations, below the stated 100,000,000 budget. That makes the candidate provisionally plausible, not approved: constants, expensive body operations, memory, language overhead, and safety margin still need review.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Reject a strategy from a concrete upper-bound calculation or an unavoidable resource limit. Do not confuse an expensive-but-required output enumeration with avoidable brute force.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_reject_cubic: Polynomial degree alone does not decide feasibility; the maximum n places this cubic count below the abstract budget.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.quadrillion: Computing 400·400·400 gives 64,000,000, not a quadrillion-scale value.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant: The feasibility check substitutes a maximum, but the algorithmic class remains cubic.

constraints: Use an abstract budget of 100,000,000 equal-cost operations and ignore constants for the first pass.

items.prompt: A proposed search checks every pair of n values, but the task must return every qualifying pair and k can be Θ(n²). What is the correct review?

options.text: Quadratic work may be unavoidable in worst cases because the required output can itself be quadratic.
Reject O(n²) without considering output.
Returning pairs always uses O(1) output space.
Rename the loops to avoid the quadratic bound.

feedback.reason: An output-sensitive problem can legitimately require a high worst-case bound.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

If k qualifying pairs can be Θ(n²), writing them already costs Ω(k) = Ω(n²) time and output space. Quadratic worst-case work is therefore not automatically avoidable. A strong algorithm should still approach input-plus-output cost and avoid checking all pairs on instances where k is small.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Reject a strategy from a concrete upper-bound calculation or an unavoidable resource limit. Do not confuse an expensive-but-required output enumeration with avoidable brute force.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_reject: The output lower bound may already be Ω(n²).
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant_output: Materializing k = Θ(n²) distinct pairs requires quadratic output storage rather than O(1).
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.names: Renaming loop variables changes no candidate pair, output requirement, or executed comparison.

items.prompt: Which observation best rejects a full O(3^n) state search for n = 30 under a 100,000,000-state budget?

options.text: 3^30 is about 206 trillion states, far above the budget.
The code must contain exactly three nested loops.
n = 30 makes every algorithm easy.
The states have long names.

feedback.reason: Concrete state-space size supplies the rejection proof.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Substitute n = 30: `3^30 = 205,891,132,094,649`, about 2.06×10^14 states. Dividing by the 10^8-state budget leaves a factor above two million, before per-state work, so constant-factor tuning cannot make the full search fit.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Reject a strategy from a concrete upper-bound calculation or an unavoidable resource limit. Do not confuse an expensive-but-required output enumeration with avoidable brute force.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.three_loops: Exponential state search need not use three loops.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.n_small: Thirty is small only as a raw integer; exponentiating it produces more than 200 trillion states.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.state_names: State labels do not alter the 3-way branching count or the resulting 3^30 search space.

constraints: Use an abstract budget of 100,000,000 states.

items.prompt: Why is "nested loops always mean brute force" an unreliable heuristic?

options.text: Nested loops may perform bounded aggregate work or implement a necessary structured computation.
Nested loops never increase runtime.
Brute force cannot be written recursively.
Only loop variable names define brute force.

feedback.reason: Brute force is about enumerating a large candidate space without enough structure, not about syntax alone.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Syntax does not reveal aggregate work. A monotonic inner pointer can advance only n times across all outer iterations, and a stack item can be pushed and popped once, so nested loops may remain linear. Conversely, exhaustive search can be expressed recursively with no visible nested loop.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Reject a strategy from a concrete upper-bound calculation or an unavoidable resource limit. Do not confuse an expensive-but-required output enumeration with avoidable brute force.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.loops_never_cost: Independent inner work that restarts for every outer iteration can multiply counts and produce quadratic or worse time.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.brute_force_no_loops: Recursive branching can enumerate the same exponential candidate space without explicit nested loop syntax.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.names: Variable names reveal neither reset behavior, aggregate movement, nor the number of generated candidates.

items.prompt: Which signs justify rejecting a candidate algorithm before implementation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Substituted dominant work exceeds the budget by orders of magnitude.
The required table or state set cannot fit the memory limit.
The algorithm explores far more candidates than the required output or decision contract demands.
The technique is unfamiliar to the reviewer.

feedback.reason: Rejection should be based on workload, resources, and contract mismatch.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

A candidate is quantitatively infeasible when substituted work or live storage exceeds the stated budgets, or structurally wasteful when it enumerates far more states than the output or decision contract requires. Reviewer familiarity says nothing about any of those measurements.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Reject a strategy from a concrete upper-bound calculation or an unavoidable resource limit. Do not confuse an expensive-but-required output enumeration with avoidable brute force.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unfamiliar: An unfamiliar technique may still have a proved feasible bound; rejection requires workload, memory, or contract evidence.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.orders_over_budget: A many-orders-of-magnitude operation gap cannot be repaired by ordinary constant-factor implementation tuning.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.memory_over_budget: A design that cannot keep its required live state within the memory limit is infeasible regardless of time.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.avoidable_output_gap: Exploring vastly more candidates than the requested answer needs signals missing structure or reuse rather than unavoidable output work.

items.prompt: Which situations can make exhaustive search reasonable? Select all that apply.

options.text: The maximum n makes the full state space fit with margin.
The contract requires materializing every candidate solution.
A small secondary parameter bounds the exponential part.
The state space is enormous and no pruning or output requirement exists.

feedback.reason: Brute force is a tool with a domain of validity.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Exhaustive search is reasonable when a concrete maximum makes the full state count fit with margin, a small parameter confines the exponential factor, or the contract itself requires all results. Without one of those bounds, an enormous state space remains a rejection case.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Reject a strategy from a concrete upper-bound calculation or an unavoidable resource limit. Do not confuse an expensive-but-required output enumeration with avoidable brute force.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.large_unbounded: An enormous unbounded state space with neither guaranteed pruning nor mandatory output has no demonstrated path to the resource budget.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.small_n: Substituting the actual maximum n can show that every state and its per-state work fit with safety margin.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_all_outputs: When every candidate solution must be materialized, enumeration is bounded below by the output volume.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.strong_parameter: A small secondary parameter can confine exponential work even when the main input size is large.

items.prompt: Which claims are insufficient to improve a brute-force worst-case bound? Select all that apply.

options.text: The implementation usually prunes many branches.
The benchmark machine is fast.
The inner loop is highly optimized.
A proof limits every search to polynomially many states.

feedback.reason: A stronger worst-case claim needs a structural proof, not typical behavior or constants.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

“Usually prunes” is an average-behavior observation, while fast hardware and micro-optimization change constants. None prevents a worst-case input from exposing the original tree. Only a proof that every input visits a smaller bounded number of states changes the worst-case class.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Reject a strategy from a concrete upper-bound calculation or an unavoidable resource limit. Do not confuse an expensive-but-required output enumeration with avoidable brute force.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.guaranteed_bound: This is sufficient to change the worst-case class.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.usually_prunes: A worst-case input may defeat every heuristic prune and expose the full original search tree.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.fast_machine: Faster hardware multiplies throughput by a constant but leaves exponential or factorial growth unchanged.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.micro_optimized: Reducing per-state constants cannot change how the number of visited states grows with n.

items.prompt: Which distinctions are needed when reviewing an expensive enumerator? Select all that apply.

options.text: Whether the task asks only for existence/count or for every result.
The maximum number and size of returned results.
Whether the algorithm generates duplicate candidates that the contract does not require.
Whether loop variables are named i and j.

feedback.reason: A brute-force label is meaningful only relative to the requested result contract.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

An existence decision may need only one witness, while listing requires every result and inherits its output lower bound. Maximum result count and record size quantify that bound. Duplicate candidates not required by the contract are avoidable exploration and must be separated from necessary outputs.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Reject a strategy from a concrete upper-bound calculation or an unavoidable resource limit. Do not confuse an expensive-but-required output enumeration with avoidable brute force.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.variable_names: Loop identifiers do not change the decision/list contract, output volume, or number of duplicate candidates generated.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.decision_vs_list: A decision problem can often stop at one witness, whereas a listing problem must materialize every valid result.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.output_size: Writing the maximum number and size of required results gives an unavoidable lower bound on time and output space.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.duplicates: Generating equivalent candidates repeatedly adds search work that the result contract does not require.

elements.text: Derive its dominant time and space expressions.
Substitute maximum constraints and output requirements.
Compare estimated work and storage with explicit budgets.
If infeasible, identify exploitable order, reuse, monotonicity, or smaller parameters.

feedback.reason: Rejection should be quantitative and followed by a search for structure.

items: Derive dominant time, auxiliary-space, and output-volume expressions for the candidate.
Substitute maximum constraints and distinguish required outputs from explored internal states.
Compare concrete totals with explicit operation and memory budgets, including a safety margin.
If infeasible, seek order, monotonicity, reuse, pruning guarantees, or a smaller parameter that changes the dominant class.

items.prompt: An algorithm enumerates all subsets for n = 40. Estimate the state count and budget fit for a 100,000,000-state budget.

feedback.reason: The state space exceeds the budget by roughly four orders of magnitude.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

`2^40 = 1,099,511,627,776`, about 1.1 trillion subset states. Dividing by the 100,000,000-state budget gives a factor of about 10,995, so the full enumeration exceeds the budget by roughly four orders of magnitude before per-state work.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Reject a strategy from a concrete upper-bound calculation or an unavoidable resource limit. Do not confuse an expensive-but-required output enumeration with avoidable brute force.

items.prompt: An algorithm enumerates all 11! permutations. Estimate the state count and whether it fits a 100,000,000-state budget before per-permutation work.

feedback.reason: The raw state count fits the abstract budget.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

`11! = 11·10·…·1 = 39,916,800`, so the raw candidate count is below 100,000,000. This is only a first-pass fit: materializing each length-11 permutation can multiply output work toward 439 million element writes, and per-state checks may remove the remaining margin.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Reject a strategy from a concrete upper-bound calculation or an unavoidable resource limit. Do not confuse an expensive-but-required output enumeration with avoidable brute force.

items.prompt: For n = 100,000, an algorithm compares every unordered pair. Estimate pair count and budget fit for 100,000,000 operations.
constraints: Use n(n - 1)/2 and ignore constant per-pair overhead.

feedback.reason: There are approximately 4,999,950,000 unordered pairs.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

The unordered-pair count is `n(n−1)/2 = 100,000·99,999/2 = 4,999,950,000`. Compared with 100,000,000 operations, the pair enumeration is about 50 times over budget before the work performed for each pair.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Reject a strategy from a concrete upper-bound calculation or an unavoidable resource limit. Do not confuse an expensive-but-required output enumeration with avoidable brute force.

items.prompt: A task must return every subset of n = 24 elements, materializing each selected-element list. Select the number of subsets and a tight asymptotic output-volume bound.
constraints: Across the full power set, each element appears in exactly half of the subsets.

feedback.reason: There are 2^n subsets, and total materialized element occurrences are n·2^(n-1).

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Each of n elements appears in exactly half of the 2^n subsets, so the materialized lists contain `n·2^(n−1)` total element occurrences. That is Θ(n·2^n), not merely Θ(2^n), because writing the contents of each selected-element list is part of the output contract. For n = 24 there are `2^24` subset lists.
